summary.heading: The molecular model and density
summary.html:
• All matter is made of particles that are always moving. Neighbours attract when slightly apart and repel strongly when pushed together.
  • Solid: fixed lattice, particles vibrate about fixed positions; fixed shape and volume. Liquid: close together but jumbled, particles slide past each other; fixed volume, takes the container's shape. Gas: far apart, fast, straight lines between collisions, almost no forces; fills the container, very low density, easy to compress.
$$\rho = \frac{m}{V}$$
  • Density in $\text{kg m}^{-3}$. $1\ \text{g cm}^{-3} = 1000\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$ and $1\ \text{cm}^3 = 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^3$.

summary.heading: Temperature and internal energy
summary.html:
$$T / \text{K} = \theta / {}^\circ\text{C} + 273$$
  • The kelvin scale is absolute: 0 K (−273 °C) is the lowest possible temperature. A temperature change is the same in K and °C. Write "300 K", not "300 °K".
  • Extending pressure–temperature lines (at constant volume) for any gas sample back to zero pressure always gives about −273 °C.
  • Kelvin temperature measures the average random kinetic energy of the particles:
$$\overline{E}_k = \frac{3}{2}k_B T$$
  • The guide states this formula for an ideal monatomic gas.
  • Internal energy = total random kinetic energy + total intermolecular potential energy of all the particles. Temperature is per particle; internal energy is the total (a warm bath has more than a cup of boiling water).
  • Net thermal energy flows from higher to lower temperature (whatever the internal energies) until thermal equilibrium: equal temperatures. "Heat" $Q$ is energy transferred because of a temperature difference; objects contain internal energy, not heat.

summary.heading: Specific heat capacity and latent heat
summary.html:
$$Q = mc\Delta T \qquad Q = mL$$
  • $c$: energy to raise 1 kg by 1 K, in $\text{J kg}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$ (water 4200, so seas warm and cool slowly).
  • $L$: energy to change the phase of 1 kg with no temperature change, in $\text{J kg}^{-1}$. $L_f$ for melting/freezing, $L_v$ for boiling/condensing. The same energy is released going the other way (why steam scalds).
  • During a phase change the energy does work against the intermolecular forces: potential energy rises, average kinetic energy (so temperature) stays constant. Flat sections on a heating curve; boiling takes longer than melting.
  • On a heating curve at constant power, gradient $= \dfrac{P}{mc}$: a steeper slope means a smaller $c$.
  • Method of mixtures (no losses): energy lost by the hot object = energy gained by the cold one; both end at the same final temperature.
  • Measuring $c$: heater energy $Q = Pt = VIt$, then $c = \dfrac{Q}{m\Delta T}$. Losses to the surroundings make the result too high; insulate.
  • Evaporation: at any temperature, from the surface only; the fastest particles escape, so the liquid left cools. Faster when warmer, larger area or with air flow. Boiling: at one temperature, throughout the liquid.
  • Names: melting, freezing, boiling (vaporization), condensing, evaporation.

summary.heading: Conduction and convection
summary.html:
• The three main mechanisms: conduction, convection, thermal radiation.
  • Conduction: faster-vibrating particles at the hot end pass kinetic energy to their neighbours in collisions; the material doesn't move. Free electrons make metals the best conductors. Gases are poor conductors, so trapped air insulates.
$$\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t} = -kA\frac{\Delta T}{\Delta x}$$
  • $k$ = thermal conductivity ($\text{W m}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$), $A$ = cross-sectional area, $\dfrac{\Delta T}{\Delta x}$ = temperature gradient. The minus sign means energy flows from hot to cold; use the size of $\Delta T$ in calculations, and $\Delta x$ in metres.
  • Metal feels colder than wood at the same temperature because its larger $k$ conducts energy from your hand faster.
  • Convection (fluids only, qualitative): heated fluid expands, its density falls and it rises; cooler, denser fluid sinks, setting up a convection current. It's the warm fluid that rises, not "heat".

summary.heading: Thermal radiation and black bodies
summary.html:
• Every object above 0 K emits electromagnetic radiation from its surface; it needs no medium. At everyday temperatures it is mostly infrared.
  • Dark, matt surfaces are good absorbers and emitters; light, shiny ones are poor at both.
  • A black body absorbs all incident radiation and is the best possible emitter at any temperature (stars are close to black bodies).
  • As $T$ rises, the black-body curve is higher at every wavelength (total power = area under it) and its peak moves to shorter wavelengths (red, then orange, then yellow-white).
$$\lambda_{\max} T = 2.9 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m K}$$
  • Wien's law: the peak wavelength gives the surface temperature. Cool stars look red, very hot stars blue-white.

summary.heading: Luminosity, intensity and apparent brightness
summary.html:
$$L = \sigma A T^4 \qquad b = \frac{L}{4\pi d^2}$$
  • Luminosity $L$: total power radiated, in W (Stefan–Boltzmann law for a black body; for a sphere $A = 4\pi R^2$). Doubling $T$ multiplies $L$ by 16. New for 2028 Luminosity means radiated power, for any body.
  • Comparing with the Sun: $\dfrac{L}{L_\odot} = \left(\dfrac{R}{R_\odot}\right)^2\left(\dfrac{T}{T_\odot}\right)^4$. Luminosities may be given in W or in $L_\odot$.
  • New for 2028 Intensity $I = \dfrac{P}{A}$: power per unit area on a surface at right angles to the radiation, in $\text{W m}^{-2}$.
  • Apparent brightness $b$: the power received per square metre at distance $d$ (New for 2028 the intensity of the star's light where it is received). It is an inverse-square law: double $d$, quarter $b$.
  • Knowing $L$ and measuring $b$ gives the distance: $d = \sqrt{\dfrac{L}{4\pi b}}$.

summary.heading: Watch out for
summary.html:
• Using °C in $\overline{E}_k = \frac{3}{2}k_BT$, $L = \sigma AT^4$ or Wien's law (only temperature changes may be in °C).
  • Confusing temperature with internal energy, or saying the temperature rises during melting or boiling.
  • Missing a stage in ice-to-steam problems: each warming stage ($mc\Delta T$) and each phase change ($mL$) separately; mixing up $L_f$ and $L_v$.
  • Leaving $\Delta x$ in cm or mm.
  • Using $\pi R^2$ instead of $4\pi R^2$ for a star's surface.
  • Confusing luminosity (W, total power emitted) with apparent brightness ($\text{W m}^{-2}$, falls with distance).
  • "Heat rises" and "the cold gets in".

Models: Which everyday observations (diffusion of a smell, dust dancing in a sunbeam, ice floating) would you use to persuade someone that particles exist and move?
The particle model treats molecules as tiny balls. Where does that picture start to fail, and does it matter for B.1?
Evidence: Rumford's cannon-boring observation was qualitative. Why was it still strong evidence against the caloric theory, and what would a supporter of caloric have replied?
Joule later measured the energy needed to warm water by stirring it. Why did a quantitative result settle the argument where Rumford could not?
Measurement: Why might physicists prefer a temperature scale defined by a fundamental constant ($k_B$) to one defined by the melting and boiling of water?
A thermometer only tells you its own temperature. What has to be true for it to tell you the temperature of something else?
Shared endeavour: Black-body radiation needed precise measurements from one group and theory from others. What does each side need from the other?
Planck called the quantum idea "an act of desperation". What does this suggest about how new ideas are accepted?

oracy.html:
Odd one out (threes, 8 minutes): each group justifies one choice, then argues for a different one. Items: 1 kg of ice at 0 °C, 1 kg of water at 0 °C, 1 kg of water at 100 °C, 1 kg of steam at 100 °C.

  • The odd one out is … because …
  • But you could also argue …
  • The other three all …

Listen for: equal temperatures mean equal average random kinetic energy of the molecules, but internal energy also includes potential energy, so the steam has the most.

Can we trust our senses?: Hands-on: students touch a metal and a wooden object, then measure both with a thermometer. Which source of knowledge do they trust more afterwards, and why?
If our senses mislead us about temperature, why do we still trust them when reading a thermometer?
Can a wrong model still be useful?: Caloric theory got mixing experiments right. What prediction would have shown it was wrong?
Engineers still talk about heat "flowing". Is it harmful to keep using the language of an abandoned model?
How can we know about things we can neve: List the assumptions needed to get a star's temperature from Wien's law (it behaves like a black body, nothing absorbs light on the way). Which would be hardest to check?
Does indirect knowledge of a star differ in kind from indirect knowledge of the past, as in history?
Does everyday language get in the way?: Collect everyday phrases about heat and cold from the class (in any language they speak). Which ones match the physics, and which mislead?
Should physics invent new words for its ideas, or reuse everyday ones with sharper meanings?
